title: How to water a Tennessee lawn in summer (hint: less often)
excerpt: Deep and twice a week beats a little every day. Here's why, and how to tell if your lawn is getting enough.
content:
The most common lawn problem we see in July isn't too little water. It's water given the wrong way: a few minutes every evening, which keeps the roots shallow and invites fungus.

Water deep, not often

Aim for about an inch a week, in two waterings. Deep water pulls the roots down, where the soil stays cooler, so the grass copes better with heat.

Water early

Between 4am and 9am. Less is lost to the sun, and the blades dry off by midday, which keeps disease away.

Do the tuna can test

Put a few empty cans on the lawn and run the sprinkler. Time how long it takes to fill them to half an inch. That's how long each watering should run.

Let it go dormant if you have to

Fescue turns straw-colored in a dry spell to protect itself. It comes back in fall. Half an inch every two weeks keeps the crowns alive.

title: Why fall, not spring, is the best time to plant in Middle Tennessee
excerpt: Warm soil, cool air and fall rain. Plants that go in now get a whole season of roots before the summer heat.
content:
Spring feels like planting season, but in Middle Tennessee the best time is late September to November. Here's why we book most new gardens for fall.

Warm soil, cool air

The soil holds summer's heat long after the air cools down, so roots keep growing while the leaves rest.

Rain does the watering

Fall brings steady rain, so new plants need far less help from the hose.

A head start on summer

A shrub planted in October has six months of root growth before the first July heat wave. One planted in May has six weeks.

Fall is for lawns too

Aerate and overseed fescue in September. The new grass gets established before winter, without competing with crabgrass.

title: Pavers or flagstone? Choosing a patio that suits your yard
excerpt: Cost, comfort, upkeep and how each one looks after ten years. A straight comparison from the people who lay both.
content:
We lay both, so we've no reason to push one. Here's how they compare.

Cost

Concrete pavers run about $24 a square foot laid. Flagstone is about $31. Natural Tennessee fieldstone, more again.

Comfort and safety

Pavers are even and flat, which is better for tables, chairs and anyone unsteady on their feet. Flagstone has more texture and is less slippery when wet.

Upkeep

Pavers with polymeric sand rarely grow weeds. Flagstone set in gravel needs weeding a couple of times a year; set in mortar, it doesn't.

How it ages

Pavers can fade a little in full sun. Flagstone gets better with age. Either way, the base underneath matters more than the stone on top.

title: When to prune: a simple calendar for the shrubs in your yard
excerpt: Prune spring bloomers after they flower, summer bloomers in late winter, and leave the oaks alone in spring.
content:
Pruning at the wrong time is the most common reason a shrub doesn't flower. This is the simple rule we follow.

Spring bloomers: right after they flower

Azaleas, forsythia and lilacs set next year's buds in summer. Prune them in late spring, as soon as the flowers fade.

Summer bloomers: late winter

Crape myrtles, butterfly bush and most roses flower on new growth. Prune them in February.

Hedges: twice a year

Late spring and late summer. Don't cut in fall, or the new growth can be hurt by frost.

Oaks: never in spring

Cuts on oaks from April to July can let in oak wilt. Wait until winter.

Not sure?

Send us a photo and we'll tell you when to cut it, free.
